passage: Felix had been in Valencia for nine days, and his Spanish stopped at "hola" and "gracias". At the hardware shop near his flat he needed wall plugs for the shelves he was fitting. He held up one finger, twisted the other hand around it, then mimed pushing something into the wall. Diego, behind the counter, nodded eagerly and came back with a box of hinges. Felix laughed and shook his head. Diego tried again: a screwdriver. Now they were both grinning, a little helpless. Felix stopped miming. He pulled out his notebook, sketched a small ribbed plug with a screw going into it and a wall behind, then held up four fingers and pointed at the sketch. "Four?" Diego asked, writing a 4 beside the drawing. "These?" He reached under the counter. Exactly right. Felix wrote "gracias" under the drawing and underlined it twice.

qa.q: What did Felix need at the hardware shop?
qa.a: Wall plugs for the shelves he was fitting.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling when Diego brought the screwdriver?
qa.a: Felix felt amused but a little helpless and frustrated, since the mime kept being read as something else.

qa.q: What fixed the misunderstanding?
qa.a: A quick sketch of the plug and screw plus a number, which Diego confirmed by writing 4 and asking 'These?' before handing it over.

passage: On her third night at the working women's hostel in Kolkata, Sudha needed to press her shirt for her first day at the lab. The warden, Gargi-di, spoke Bangla and some Hindi; Sudha's Hindi was shaky and her Bangla non-existent. At the office window, Sudha pinched her collar, then slid her flat palm back and forth over an invisible surface. Gargi-di's face lit up. She reached behind her and handed over a mop and bucket. Sudha burst out laughing, and so did Gargi-di, though neither knew exactly why yet. Sudha set the mop down, found a picture of an iron on her phone and held it up next to her creased sleeve. "Istri!" Gargi-di said. "Istri?" Sudha repeated carefully, pointing at the photo. Gargi-di nodded, unlocked a cupboard and brought out an iron. "Ten o'clock, back," she said, tapping her watch.

qa.q: What did Gargi-di hand over first?
qa.a: A mop and bucket.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she was handed the mop?
qa.a: Sudha felt amused and a bit sheepish 😅, realising the pressing mime looked like floor cleaning, with some worry underneath about the creased shirt for her first day.

qa.q: What helped Sudha get the right thing?
qa.a: Showing a picture of an iron next to her creased sleeve and repeating the word 'Istri' back to confirm it.

qa.a: Gargi-di read it as wiping or mopping, a sensible guess from the gesture alone, which is why a picture helped.

passage:
Hi Darshan,
You asked how I'm managing in Busan with about twelve words of Korean. Mostly with my hands, which went badly on Sunday.
I needed a big cooking pot, the kind for rice for eight people when my team comes over. At the market I made a huge circle with both arms and then stirred the air. The shop owner nodded and pulled out a plastic washing tub. I shook my head, pointed at my mouth and mimed eating. He brought out a steamer basket.
So I stopped, typed "large cooking pot" into my translation app, and showed him a photo of Ammi's big pot from my gallery. He laughed, said a word I didn't catch, and brought the right one. Before paying, I pointed at it and said, "This one, yes?" He nodded.
Lesson: hands start the conversation, pictures finish it.
Afreen

qa.a: A plastic washing tub.

Wednesday: Her draft arrived. The logo was tiny, tucked into a corner, and flat. Eshaan stared at it, confused and ready to type an irritated reply. Then it clicked: she had never seen his hands.
Friday: This time he didn't wave at the camera. He shared his screen, opened a blank page and sketched a banner with a big arched logo, then typed: "Logo width: about a third of the banner. Curved upwards." "Oh!" Gopika laughed. "On my side you just kept moving your shoulders." The next draft was exactly right.

passage: Abhinav, I saw you describing that bracket with your hands on the call just now, and the vendor's screen was frozen for half of it. Let me, Arohi, tell you a story. In my first year as a design engineer, the internet at our Shillong office was terrible. I was explaining a pipe joint to the workshop in Coimbatore: "It bends like this, then narrows like this," my hands doing all the work. The video kept freezing and jumping. The foreman nodded politely. Two weeks later a crate arrived with forty joints bent the wrong way. I remember sitting on that crate feeling sick. After that I never described a shape with my hands alone on a call. I'd hold a sketch up to the camera, send a photo of it in the chat, and ask them to tell me back what they understood. Try it this afternoon.

qa.a: Forty joints.

qa.a: Arohi felt sick with dismay and probably some guilt, realising the frozen video had hidden the hand descriptions the foreman needed.

qa.a: Arohi stopped relying on hand shapes alone, held up a sketch, sent a photo of it in the chat and asked the workshop to repeat back what they understood.

qa.a: The foreman likely saw a jumping, frozen picture and caught only fragments, but nodded politely, perhaps not wanting to seem slow or to question the engineer.

passage: Hafsa's laptop camera had died that morning, so she joined the call on her phone, propped against a mug, with nine percent battery. Arnab, the new intern, was setting up the conference hall for Saturday's workshop and needed the seating plan. "Tables in a horseshoe, like this," Hafsa said, curving both hands into a U. On Arnab's screen, the phone showed only her forehead and the ceiling fan. "Like... a circle?" he asked. "No, open at the front. Like this!" She made the U bigger. The picture froze, then jumped. Arnab looked more lost. Seven percent. Hafsa stopped gesturing. She grabbed a sticky note, drew a U with little squares for tables and an arrow marked "stage", and held it right up to the camera. Then she typed in the chat: "U shape, open end facing the stage, 12 tables." "Oh, a horseshoe!" Arnab said. "Got it." The screen went black.

qa.a: 12 tables.

passage: Sumit here, from the next cubicle. For the whole of March, Nikita sat curled over her laptop like a question mark, nose almost at the screen, from nine till well past seven. Our team lead, passing once, muttered, "She looks half asleep." I didn't know what to think. Was she exhausted? Just deep in the data migration? Last Thursday she stood up and pressed both hands into her lower back, wincing. "My neck's been killing me for weeks," she said, to nobody in particular. The next Monday things changed. She'd raised her chair, stacked two old binders under the laptop so the screen sat at eye level, and every hour a little alarm made her stand and walk to the window and back. By Wednesday she was sitting straighter and laughing at my jokes again. The migration finished two days early.

qa.q: What did Nikita stack under the laptop?
qa.a: Two old binders, so the screen sat at eye level.

qa.q: What might Nikita's curled-over posture have meant during March?
qa.a: It likely showed focus mixed with growing tiredness and discomfort, since she winced and said her neck had hurt for weeks; it was not the half-asleep laziness the team lead assumed.

qa.q: Which changes helped Nikita, and why?
qa.a: Raising the chair, lifting the screen to eye level and walking every hour eased the neck strain and seemed to lift her mood too.

qa.q: How did the team lead read Nikita's posture, and what did that miss?
qa.a: The team lead read it as looking half asleep, missing that she was working long hours on the migration and was in pain.

passage:
Week one, Friday: By evening Kalyani's back felt like wet cardboard. Twelve hours a day hunched over the laptop on the dining table of her rented flat in Hyderabad. When she video-called Madhav, her colleague, he joked, "You look like you're sleeping on the keyboard. Bored?" She wasn't bored; she was sore, and too tired to explain.
Week two, Tuesday: She put the laptop on a shoebox, found a cushion for her lower back, and set a timer to stand every forty-five minutes. The first day felt fussy and slow.
Week three, Monday: Her back ached less. On the call, Madhav said, "You look more awake." This time she told him: "I was never lazy. My neck was wrecked. Shoebox and timer." Madhav winced. "Sorry about the bored comment." The next day he sent her a photo of his own laptop, perched on two cookbooks.

passage: Chaitanya, you've been bent over that laptop since nine, and I heard Mr. Batra call you lazy when you put your head down at lunch. Let me, Farida, tell you something. At twenty-three I was a typist in a newspaper office in Lucknow. Eight hours hunched over a heavy typewriter, shoulders round like a tortoise. By evening I'd rest my forehead on the desk, and the chief sub-editor told everyone I was napping on duty. I wasn't. My back burned. It was old Mr. D'Cruz, the proofreader, who saw me wincing. He put two telephone directories under my typewriter, raised my chair, and made me walk to the window with him every hour to look at the street. "The body's not lazy," he said. "It's complaining." Within a month I was sitting straight. So get up. Walk with me to the tea counter.

qa.a: Two telephone directories.

Mentoring note, week 6. Written by Elizabeth, graduate programme mentor, Leeds office.
Baljeet told me today that she had been dreading her one-to-ones with Graham, the director. "He leans right back with his hands behind his head while I talk," she said. "At home, that would mean he doesn't care." In her last job in Chandigarh, she said, senior people sat very upright and juniors stood.
I have watched Graham with her for six weeks. The lean-back is how he sits with everyone, including the chief executive. More telling: he has read every draft she has sent and forwarded her analysis to the board with her name on it.
I shared this with Baljeet and suggested she judge him by what he does over time rather than how he sits. She laughed and said, "So the lean-back isn't an insult?"
Next step: we will review in a month how the one-to-ones feel.

qa.a: In Chandigarh.

qa.a: She felt dread and some hurt, reading his lean-back as not caring, based on how seniors sat in her last job.

qa.a: To judge Graham by what he does over time rather than how he sits, since reading her drafts and crediting her to the board show real interest.

qa.a: Elizabeth sees the lean-back as simply his habit with everyone, even the chief executive, not a sign of disrespect toward Baljeet.

passage:
Thursday, late
New boss, day four. Sunaina ma'am does this thing: when she comes to your desk she stands right beside the chair, close enough that I can smell her coffee, and looks down at the screen. In meetings she sits bolt upright at the head of the table and never leans back. This morning my first thought was: she's checking on me, she doesn't trust me. My shoulders were up round my ears till lunch.
But then at six, when my report crashed, she pulled a chair over, sat next to me at the same height, and spent forty minutes fixing the formulas with me. She even laughed at my terrible file names.
So what does the standing close mean? Control? Or just how she works? Honestly, I don't know yet. Four days isn't enough. I'll watch what she does for a month before I decide.
Omkar

"You've walked past me eleven times," Ayesha said from the bench outside the interview room.
Divyansh stopped mid-stride. "Sorry. Am I annoying you?"
"Not annoying. I just wondered if you were impatient or scared."
"Scared. My hands are ice." He started pacing again. "If I sit, my leg bounces like a sewing machine."
"Same. I'm Ayesha, by the way. Second round for the analyst role?"
"Divyansh. Yes. Nine forty-five."
"Mine's at ten. Want to go and stand by the stairs window? More air, fewer people watching."
They walked to the landing. Divyansh put his palms on the cool sill and took a long breath in, a longer one out.
"Better?" she asked.
"A bit. Walking helps more than sitting stiff and pretending I'm calm."
Down the corridor the door opened. "Divyansh Mehra?"
He rolled his shoulders once. "Wish me luck."
"Luck. Go."

qa.a: Nine forty-five.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's pacing mean, according to him?
qa.a: He was scared, not impatient, with icy hands and a bouncing leg, and pacing helped burn off the nervous energy.

qa.q: What helped Divyansh more than sitting still?
qa.a: Stepping away to the stairs window, putting his palms on the cool sill and taking long, slow breaths.

qa.q: How did Ayesha read the pacing before she asked?
qa.a: Ayesha couldn't tell whether it was impatience or fear, so instead of guessing she asked, and it turned out she felt the same nerves.

subtype: Restless pacing at work or in waiting rooms [Regulating]
passage: The morning they announced the restructuring, I couldn't sit. Our whole team had fifteen-minute slots with HR, in alphabetical order, and mine was after lunch. So I paced: water cooler, window, printer, water cooler. Disha, whose desk I kept circling, finally looked up. "Lalit, you're making me dizzy. Can you not be so impatient?" It stung, because I wasn't impatient. I was terrified. I just didn't have the words for it then. I went downstairs and walked round the block twice, slowly, breathing in for four steps and out for six, past the chai stall and the bus stop. By the time I came back, my chest wasn't so tight. My slot came. My role was moving to another team, not ending. Later I told Disha the pacing had been fear. She said, "I thought you were cross with me for being slow."

qa.a: Lalit felt hurt and misunderstood, because the pacing came from fear about the restructuring, not impatience.

passage:
Family support note, outpatient waiting area, 14 February. Written by Kavitha, hospital social worker.
Ira, the patient's daughter, arrived at ten for her father's results meeting. For forty minutes she paced the corridor, from the lift to the fire door and back, checking her phone each time. Two other families glanced at her; one woman muttered about her being impatient. I did not think it was impatience. Her jaw was tight and her breathing was fast and shallow.
I didn't ask her to sit down. I asked, "Would it help to step outside for a few minutes? I'll come and get you the moment the doctor is ready." She nodded. We walked to the garden. I suggested slowing her out-breath; she did, and her shoulders came down.
When the doctor called, she walked in steadier.
Next step: I will check in with Ira after the meeting, whatever the news.

qa.q: How long did Ira pace the corridor?
qa.a: For forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Kavitha think Ira's pacing showed, and why?
qa.a: Kavitha read it as fear and anxiety, not impatience, because of Ira's tight jaw and fast, shallow breathing.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha offer a walk outside instead of asking Ira to sit down?
qa.a: Moving and slowing her breath in the garden let Ira burn off nervous energy, while sitting rigid would have kept it bottled up; the promise to fetch her made leaving feel safe.

qa.q: How might the woman who muttered have seen Ira differently?
qa.a: If she had noticed the tight jaw and fast breathing, she might have felt sympathy, seeing a frightened daughter rather than an impatient one.

grounding: A social worker notes a young adult pacing before hard news, others reading it as impatience, and a short walk with slower breathing helping.

subtype: Walking away in conflict at work [Regulating]
passage:
Tuesday night
Walked out on Sonali today. Properly walked out. We were arguing about who dropped the client follow-up, and she said, "You always do this," and I felt something hot come up my throat. I knew if I opened my mouth I'd say something about her last project that I couldn't take back. So I just stood up and left. No word. The door swung shut behind me.
Twenty minutes on the terrace, breathing, and I was okay. But when I came back, Sonali wouldn't look at me. Rakesh told me later she thought I'd walked out on her like she wasn't worth answering.
Fair. From her side, that's exactly what it looked like.
Tomorrow: go to her desk first thing. Say I left because I was about to say something unkind, not because she didn't matter. And next time, say "I need ten minutes, I'll come back" BEFORE leaving.
Sumit

qa.q: Where did Sumit spend twenty minutes?
qa.a: On the terrace, breathing.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling just before walking out?
qa.a: Sumit felt a hot surge of anger and feared saying something unkind about Sonali's last project that couldn't be taken back.

qa.q: What does Sumit plan to do differently?
qa.a: Go to Sonali first thing to explain why Sumit left, and next time say 'I need ten minutes, I'll come back' before walking out.

qa.q: How did Sonali experience the walk-out?
qa.a: She felt disrespected and hurt, as if she wasn't worth answering, so she wouldn't look at Sumit afterwards.

subtype: Walking away in conflict at work [Regulating]
passage: The panchayat office in Karnal district was hot and crowded, and the argument about the self-help group's register had gone round three times. Payal, who kept the ledger, jabbed a finger at the page. "You never check anything, Minakshi, and then you blame me." Minakshi felt her face go hot. A sharp reply was already in her mouth, the kind about Payal's spelling that would sting for months. Instead she held up a palm. "I'm too angry to talk well right now. I'm going to walk to the handpump and back. Ten minutes. Then let's finish." Payal blinked, arms crossed. The women on the bench exchanged looks. Minakshi walked out into the sun, drank from the handpump and let the anger slow. When she returned, she sat beside Payal, not across. "Show me where the numbers don't match. I'll listen properly." Payal uncrossed her arms.

qa.a: To the handpump and back.

passage:
Saturday: Outside the metro station, a drunk man started shouting at Raghav for bumping into him. Chaitanya stepped between them, chest out, fists half closed. "Back off!" The man shoved Chaitanya, and a crowd gathered. Only a passing guard pulling them apart stopped a real fight.
Sunday: Chaitanya's hands still shook over breakfast. "I wanted to protect you," Chaitanya told Raghav, "and I nearly got us both hurt." Raghav nodded. "Next time just pull me away. We walk. We call someone."
Three weeks later, Friday: At the crowded Durga Puja pandal, a man was pushing and yelling in the queue, right beside a little girl who had lost hold of her mother's hand. This time Chaitanya didn't square up, but crouched, spoke softly to the girl, and with Raghav guided her away from the pushing to the volunteers' desk. Raghav told the police constable there about the man. The girl's mother came running within minutes.

qa.a: Chaitanya felt shaken and regretful, hands still trembling, realising the urge to protect Raghav had nearly got them both hurt.

passage: Ishita, you asked what I'd do if the crowd at your concert turned rough. Let me, Seema, tell you about the river fair trip. I was twenty-four, a new teacher, with eleven Class 7 students on the ghats. Suddenly a group of young men came shoving down the steps, shouting, knocking people aside. My first instinct was to plant myself in front of the children, arms out, and shout back. I even opened my mouth. Then I saw one of them swinging a bamboo stick. Shouting would only turn him toward us. So I pulled the children against the wall in a tight line, holding the smallest boy's hand, and we moved sideways, step by step, to the police tent. I told the constable what I'd seen, and two officers went down the steps. Then we counted heads. Eleven. I have never counted so carefully in my life.

qa.q: How many students was Seema responsible for?
qa.a: Eleven Class 7 students.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when the young men came shoving down the steps?
qa.a: Seema felt a rush of fear and protective anger, wanting to shout back, until the bamboo stick turned it into careful caution.

qa.q: What choice in the story kept the children safe?
qa.a: Moving them in a tight line along the wall to the police tent and telling the constable, rather than confronting the group.

qa.q: What might the smallest boy have felt as Seema held his hand?
qa.a: He was probably scared by the shouting and shoving but felt safer holding on as they moved together.

grounding: An elder recalls wanting to shield children by confronting a rough crowd and choosing instead to move them away and alert the police.

passage: The rain had turned the side road in Andheri into a stream, and Imran's phone had died at the office party. He and Sarika were walking to the station when a man on a scooter slowed beside them, calling out to Sarika, then circled back a second time. Imran felt his whole body tighten. He moved to walk on the road side, between Sarika and the scooter, and caught himself squaring his shoulders. Part of him wanted to shout, even to grab the handlebar. Then he saw how empty the street was. "Chemist, left," he said quietly. They ducked into the lit shop. Sarika's phone still had battery; she called the police helpline while Imran asked the chemist if they could wait inside. The chemist pulled the shutter halfway down and let them stay. Ten minutes later a patrol jeep pulled up, and the scooter was gone.

qa.q: Why couldn't Imran use his phone?
qa.a: His phone had died at the office party.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when the scooter circled back?
qa.a: Imran felt tense, protective and angry, even tempted to grab the handlebar, but also wary because the street was empty.

qa.a: It moved them to a lit place with other people and let Sarika call the police helpline, instead of a confrontation that could have escalated.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sarika during this?
qa.a: Sarika was likely frightened by the man's comments and relieved that Imran stayed calm, which left room for her to call the helpline herself.

grounding: Shows a young adult's urge to step between a friend and a threat, and the wiser choice of moving to safety and calling the police.

passage: Kashish came back to the insurance office three weeks after the bus crash on the highway, and everyone said she looked fine. But the floor was being renovated, and every time a drill screamed or a hammer banged, she jumped in her seat, hands flying to the desk edge. She ate lunch alone at her screen and answered questions without looking up. Some people decided she'd gone cold. Pradeep, at the next desk, noticed she flinched most at sudden noise, not at people. He didn't ask what had happened on the bus. On Friday, when the drilling started again, he said quietly, "The meeting room on the fourth floor is quiet this week. I've booked it for our team work, if you'd rather sit there." She nodded. Later, at the lift, he added, "The office has a counsellor on Wednesdays. People go for all sorts of things. No pressure." She gave a small, tired smile.

qa.q: When is the office counsellor available?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: What might Kashish's jumping at noises and looking down suggest?
qa.a: It may reflect fear and lingering shock after the crash, or deep exhaustion; it doesn't mean she had 'gone cold' as some assumed.

qa.q: How did Pradeep support Kashish without pushing?
qa.a: He didn't ask about the crash, offered a quiet room away from the drilling, and gently mentioned the counsellor with no pressure.

qa.q: How did some colleagues misread Kashish?
qa.a: They decided she had gone cold, reading her withdrawal as unfriendliness instead of possible fear or exhaustion.

grounding: Shows a young professional startling and withdrawing after a hard event, and a colleague offering patience and professional help without pushing.

passage: Since Vandana left the consulting job in October, the flat in Lajpat Nagar had gone quiet. She slept late, kept her door half closed, and when Neelam asked about her day, her eyes slid to the floor. The phone buzzing made her jump. Neelam's mother, calling from Jaipur, said, "Sit her down and make her talk. She'll feel better." Neelam didn't. She had tried once, and Vandana had gone even quieter. Instead she left a plate of poha outside the door each morning and sat in the living room in the evenings with the television low, just in case. One night Vandana came out and sat at the other end of the sofa. After a while she said, "I think I'm really burnt out." Neelam nodded. "Do you want me to help you find someone to talk to? A counsellor?" Vandana was quiet, then said, "Maybe. Yes."

qa.q: What did Neelam leave outside the door each morning?
qa.a: A plate of poha.

qa.q: What might Vandana's sliding eyes and jumping at the phone suggest?
qa.a: They may show exhaustion and stress after the job, perhaps low mood too; it might look like coldness, but she seems worn down.

qa.q: Why was Neelam's approach better than 'make her talk'?
qa.a: Pushing had made Vandana quieter, while steady presence and small kindnesses let her come out when ready, and then Neelam offered help finding a counsellor.

qa.a: She thinks talking will fix it and wants Neelam to push, not seeing that pressure made Vandana withdraw further.

grounding: Shows a young professional withdrawing after burnout and a flatmate offering patience and professional help instead of pushing her to open up.

passage:
"Uma, got a minute? Just us."
Uma followed Minakshi into the small meeting room, eyes on her own shoes.
"You don't have to tell me anything," Minakshi said. "I only wanted to check how you're doing since you came back."
"Fine." A pause. "Sorry. I know I've been quiet."
"Nothing to be sorry for. You lost your father six weeks ago."
Uma's jaw tightened. She stared at the window.
"I won't ask you to talk about it," Minakshi said. "Two things only. First, if mornings are hard, you can start at eleven for a while. Second, the company has a counselling line. Grief is one of the things they help with. I'll send you the number, and you can ignore it if you want."
Uma nodded slowly. "People keep asking me to share how I feel."
"You don't owe anyone that."
"Thank you." For the first time, she looked up.

qa.q: How long ago did Uma's father die?
qa.a: Six weeks ago.

qa.q: What might Uma's eyes on her shoes and tight jaw suggest?
qa.a: They likely show grief and strain, maybe tiredness from people asking her to share; they don't mean she is unfriendly or uninterested.

qa.q: What did Minakshi offer, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: A later start time and the counselling line number with no pressure to use it, giving practical support and professional help without pushing Uma to open up.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Uma finally looks up?
qa.a: Minakshi may feel relieved and quietly moved, seeing that patience rather than pressure has let Uma trust her a little.

grounding: Shows a grieving young professional avoiding eye contact and a manager offering patience and professional help instead of pushing.

passage:
Dear Maria,
I owe you an explanation for Saturday. At your engagement dinner I was on my phone half the night: tapping, scrolling, checking. I saw your face when you were telling everyone how Joel proposed and I was looking at my screen. You must have thought I didn't care. I'm so sorry.
The truth is, my younger brother was taken to the emergency ward that afternoon after a fall at cricket, and my parents were sending updates. I didn't want to spoil your night by announcing it, so I kept checking quietly. But I should have told you in one line: "Family thing, I may need to check my phone." That would have taken five seconds and saved you from wondering.
He's fine now, a cracked wrist and a sulk.
Can I take you for coffee this week and hear the proposal story properly, phone in my bag?
Love,
Nirmala

qa.q: Why were Nirmala's parents sending updates?
qa.a: Nirmala's younger brother had been taken to the emergency ward after a fall at cricket.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling while checking the phone at the dinner?
qa.a: Nirmala was anxious about the brother and torn, not wanting to spoil Maria's night; the scrolling came from worry, not boredom.

qa.q: What does Nirmala say would have prevented the hurt?
qa.a: A one-line explanation at the start, 'Family thing, I may need to check my phone', so Maria wouldn't have read the scrolling as not caring.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt while telling the proposal story?
qa.a: Maria probably felt hurt and a bit ignored, seeing her friend looking at a screen during an important moment.

grounding: Shows a young adult's phone-checking read as disrespect when it came from worry, and how a short explanation would have prevented hurt.

passage: Okay, Siddharth, you want to know why I put my phone face down now? It started at my cousin's mehendi. I'm Kalyani, and I don't know half my relatives, so whenever the talk stopped I'd grab my phone and scroll. Not reading anything. Just something to hold, so I didn't look lost. Then Chitra Mausi, who'd come all the way from Nagpur, sat next to me and started telling me about her new house. Mid-sentence, a silence came, and my thumb went to the screen. She stopped talking. Later my mother told me Mausi thought I found her boring. I felt awful. It was the opposite; I was nervous and didn't know what to say. So the next day I went and told her, "Mausi, I fiddle with my phone when I'm shy. It's not you." She laughed and pinched my cheek. Now the phone stays in my bag.

qa.q: Where had Chitra Mausi come from?
qa.a: All the way from Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when reaching for the phone at the mehendi?
qa.a: Kalyani felt shy and nervous in the silences, not knowing many relatives, and used the phone to avoid looking lost.

qa.q: What repaired the hurt with Chitra Mausi?
qa.a: Going to her the next day and explaining that the phone-fiddling comes from shyness, not boredom with her.

qa.q: How did Chitra Mausi read the phone-scrolling?
qa.a: She took it as a sign that Kalyani found her boring and felt hurt enough to stop talking.

grounding: Shows a young adult scrolling a phone for comfort in awkward silences, a relative reading it as boredom, and a short explanation repairing it.

passage: I'm Madhuri, and I was at the team's farewell lunch for Mrs. Kulkarni at the Irani café. Halfway through her speech, Sachin, across from me, had his phone out under the table, thumb flying. A couple of people exchanged looks. Someone whispered, "Couldn't wait an hour?" Honestly, I was irritated too; Mrs. Kulkarni had trained him. But his leg was jiggling and he kept biting his lip, which didn't look like boredom. When the speech ended, before anyone could say anything, he stood up. "I'm really sorry about the phone. The payment server went down twenty minutes ago and I'm on call. I've handed it over now." He walked round and took Mrs. Kulkarni's hand in both of his. "I heard most of your speech. Thank you for everything." The looks around the table softened. I still don't know whether he heard the part about him.

qa.q: Where was the farewell lunch?
qa.a: At the Irani café.

qa.q: What did Sachin's jiggling leg and bitten lip suggest while he tapped the phone?
qa.a: They suggested anxiety and urgency rather than boredom; he was stressed about the server outage, though Madhuri couldn't be sure at the time.

qa.q: What prevented the hurt from lasting?
qa.a: Sachin explained briefly that he was on call for a server outage, then thanked Mrs. Kulkarni directly.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel about the phone at first?
qa.a: Madhuri felt irritated on Mrs. Kulkarni's behalf, since she had trained Sachin, though the jiggling leg made Madhuri doubt it was boredom.

grounding: An observer describes a young adult's phone use at a farewell read as disrespect when it was urgent work, and a short explanation easing it.

passage: By the third hour of the planning meeting in the Buenos Aires office, Camila was rubbing her temples in slow circles, eyes half closed. Every few minutes her hand moved to the back of her neck and squeezed. Tomas, sitting beside her, couldn't tell what it meant. Was she exhausted from the night flight from Córdoba? Tense about the targets slide, which was hers? Or did she just have a headache? The director was already on slide forty. Tomas leaned over and said quietly, "Want me to ask for a ten-minute break?" Camila opened her eyes, surprised, then nodded. "Please. My head is pounding." Tomas raised his hand. "Could we take ten? The coffee's getting cold." Nobody objected; a few people stretched with obvious relief. Camila went out to the balcony, drank a full glass of water and came back looking less pinched.

qa.q: Which slide was Camila's?
qa.a: The targets slide.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling during the third hour?
qa.a: Camila was tired and in discomfort with a pounding head; Tomas had also wondered whether she was tense about her targets slide.

qa.q: Why was Tomas's offer a good way to respond?
qa.a: He asked quietly instead of guessing, and framed the break for the whole room, so Camila got relief without being singled out.

qa.q: How did the rest of the room react to the break?
qa.a: Nobody objected and several people stretched with obvious relief, suggesting they were tired too.

grounding: Shows a young professional rubbing temples and neck in a long meeting, a colleague unable to tell why, and a kind offer of a break.

subtype: Rubbing temples and neck at work [Expressing]
passage: The Saturday staff meeting at the municipal school in Pune had run past two hours, and the fan above Irawati's chair only pushed the hot air around. She sat at the back, one hand kneading the side of her neck, then pressing two fingers into her temple. Vandana, the head teacher, noticed from the front. A senior teacher leaned over and murmured, "The young ones never pay attention." Vandana didn't answer. She finished the agenda item, then called a five-minute break for water. As people filed out, she stopped by Irawati's chair. "You've been rubbing your neck a lot. Tired, or is something hurting?" Irawati looked startled, then embarrassed. "Both, I think. I've had three extra classes this week and I've been marking late every night." Vandana nodded. "Let's look at those extra classes on Monday."

qa.q: How many extra classes had Irawati taken this week?
qa.a: Three extra classes.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Vandana asked about her neck?
qa.a: Irawati felt startled and a bit embarrassed at being noticed, then admitted to being both tired and sore.

qa.q: What did Vandana do instead of accepting the senior teacher's view?
qa.a: She called a short break for everyone and then asked Irawati kindly whether she was tired or hurting, rather than assuming inattention.

qa.q: How did the senior teacher read Irawati's gestures?
qa.a: The senior teacher saw a young teacher not paying attention, missing the possibility of tiredness or pain.

grounding: Shows a young teacher rubbing neck and temples in a long meeting and a head teacher asking kindly instead of guessing.

passage:
Hi Pranav,
Thanks for your message after the client review, and for asking instead of assuming. You're right that I was rubbing my temples and the back of my neck for most of the second half. I realise that in front of the client it might have looked like I was bored, or annoyed with their feedback.
It wasn't either. I'd slept badly after the late deployment on Wednesday, and by eleven I had a thick headache sitting behind my eyes. I didn't want to interrupt the meeting to say so, which was probably a mistake.
If it happens again, I'll just say, "Sorry, bit of a headache, give me a moment," and step out for water. Much better than letting people guess.
And I'm fine today, properly slept.
Thanks again for checking,
Ramesh

qa.q: When was the late deployment?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel during the second half of the client review?
qa.a: Ramesh felt tired and in discomfort with a thick headache, and was also a little worried that the gestures looked like boredom or annoyance.

qa.q: What does Ramesh plan to do next time?
qa.a: Say briefly that there's a headache and step out for water, so people don't have to guess what the gesture means.

qa.q: How might the client have read Ramesh's temple-rubbing?
qa.a: The client might have taken it as boredom or annoyance with their feedback, since the gesture alone doesn't show it was a headache.
